text: 330 W. 20th Avenue City Attorney's Office San Mateo, CA 94403 (650) 522-7020 www.cityofsanmateo.org
City AttorneVs Impartial Analysis of Measure

The City of San Mateo currently imposes a transactions and use tax, commonly known as a sales tax, of 0.25%. If voters approve Measure it would increase this tax from 0.25% to 0.50%. A 0.25% increase amounts to an extra 25 cents per $100 purchased. The additional 0.25% sales tax would remain in effect until voters end it. Measure will be adopted if approved by a majority of voters voting on it. If voters approve it, the proposed tax is estimated to generate approximately $7 million a year in locally controlled funding. Measure would be a general tax, which means that the tax revenue could be spent for any City purpose, which includes maintenance of local streets, parks, and other infrastructure, as well as police, fire, paramedic, crime prevention, 9-1-1 emergency response, and traffic safety improvements. The tax would not apply to groceries or prescription medication, among other exceptions provided by state law.

Under state law, the combined rate of all such taxes imposed by the City and San Mateo County is capped at 2%, and there is remaining capacity within this cap of one-quarter percent (0.25%). The City is authorized to impose this tax with voter approval. On July 20, 2026, the San Mateo City Council voted to place Measure on the ballot.

The State would collect tax revenue under a contract with the City, and pay it to the City. Measure would require an annual audit and provide for a committee of five members of the public to review and report on receipts and spending of tax proceeds.
If voters approve it, the tax would be collected starting with the first day of the calendar quarter starting 110 days after the City Council certifies election results.
A YES vote approves the measure.
Prasanna W. Rasiah City Attorney

text: Rebuttal to Argument Against the San Mateo Sales Tax Measure
We agree on one thing: every tax dollar must be spent responsibly. However, fiscal responsibility also means confronting reality and not allowing the services we depend on to deteriorate.

Measure H asks for an additional 1/4$ to protect the basics that keep San Mateo safe and strong: police and fire protection, paramedics and 911 response, safer streets and pothole repair, clean parks and other essential city services.

Opponents argue that approximately $7 million won't eliminate the projected deficit, which is now $18.2 million. But rejecting $7 million because it doesn't solve every problem means the city will have to make more significant cuts that affect our everyday lives. Measure H is about the people who coach your child's Little League team, who make Music in the Park happen, who respond to the 17-year-old's cardiac arrest fast enough to save their life and so much more.
We should demand efficiency and accountability City Hall. Yet efficiency alone doesn't fill potholes, answer 91 1 calls, or ensure firefighters and paramedics are there when our families need them.
We should insist on accountability and protect essential services. An oversight committee will continue reviewing how funds are allocated and spent, providing transparency and public accountability.
And let's be clear: this measure will not increase the cost of groceries or prescription medications, which are exempt from sales tax.
Measure H is a practical investment in the city we all call home—while demanding responsible stewardship of every dollar.
Vote YES on Measure H for a safe, strong, and fiscally responsible San Mateo.
FILED OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTIONS OFFICER SAN MATEO CCUNIY
